catalog_quote: SOUND CHANGE PROBLEM 8 PMP to Mukah Melanau (coastal Sarawak, Malaysian Borneo) Background. 'Melanau' is a dialect chain that stretches about 180 miles along the coast of Sarawak in Malaysian Borneo, from Balingian in the north to the mouth of the Rejang River in the south, and from there upriver to Kanowit, about 100 miles inland. There is a considerable phonological variation in Melanau speech communities, much of it shared with Mukah, but some of it fairly different. In all of these communities for which field data are available stress follows a pattern similar to that of Malay, falling on the penultimate vowel unless that vowel is schwa followed by a single consonant, in which case it shifts rightward to the last syllable. Malay influence is strong in the vocabulary, and some words cited here probably are Malay loans.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. The 'file' is not the book but Google Books legacy-feed snippet XML for Blust 2018, 101 Problems and Solutions in Historical Linguistics (EUP; vol ids hHxJEAAAQBAJ ISBN 9781474429221 and 7N-fEQAAQBAJ ISBN 9781474429238). I re-parsed every saved snippet (gbk21-25, gbk31-35, gbk12, gbk14). The quoted Background passage of 'SOUND CHANGE PROBLEM 8 PMP to Mukah Melanau (coastal Sarawak, Malaysian Borneo)' is attested verbatim as a chain of overlapping snippets: gbk35 (heading + "'Melanau' is a dialect chain that stretches about 180 miles along the coast of Sarawak in Malaysian Borneo, from"), gbk32 ("mouth of the Rejang River in the south, and from there upriver…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Across the Melanau dialect chain (defined as running from Balingian to the Rejang mouth and upriver to Kanowit), stress falls on the penultimate syllable; if the penultimate vowel is schwa followed by a single consonant, stress falls on the final syllable instead. Applicability to Kanowit is by inclusion in 'all of these communities for which field data are available' (Blust had Kanowit data from Angki Kaboy, 1969-70), not by name. The same rule is stated first-hand for Mukah (Central Melanau) in Blust 1988:178-179, with two further sub-rules (final high vowel after /a/ stressed; optional final stress when a glottal stop follows the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate schwa followed by a single consonant -> final stress. (For Mukah, Blust 1988 adds: /a/+final high vowel -> final stress; optional final stress when penult is followed by glottal stop.)
new_statements.domain_note: Chain-wide generalisation in a workbook background note; Blust 1988's Mukah rule is explicitly for citation forms, and Blust 2013 remarks that coastal Sarawak languages tend to be oxytone in citation but paroxytone in phrases. No Kanowit- or Tanjong-specific statement exists in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: No source states stress for Kanowit or Tanjong by name. The quoted Blust 2018 sentence is a generalisation over the whole Melanau dialect chain (explicitly said to reach 'upriver to Kanowit') in the background to a problem on Mukah Melanau; the first-hand rule it echoes (Blust 1988:178-179) is for Mukah = Central Melanau (cent2101), not kano1244. Norfazila 2025 describes the Kanowit variant proper (Kanowit district informants) but is segmental only. Tanjong (Kapit; former ISO [tnj], merged into kxn in 2008) has no phonological description beyond Chou 2002 as summarised by Rensch 2012.
